# Tall vs wide data

From the first day:

* Arrange your data so that each row is a single observation, each column is a variable ("tidy" data)

---
layout: true

# A wide data example

```{r read_tree, echo = FALSE}
trees = read.csv("data/tree_abundance.csv")
head(trees)
```
---

* Abundances of five tree species
* Note that the format of the data makes some analyses easy
	- What is the average abundance for *Abies balsamifera* across all years?

---
* But other things are harder 
	- What is the average of all species combined for each year? 
	- What is the average for each species among years?
---
* Arrange your data so that each row is a single observation, each column is a variable ("tidy" data)
* This dataset violates this principle!
	- `abundance` is spread across five colums.
	- `species` is a variable but not a column!
---
layout: false

# Converting from wide to tall

* An add-on package, `reshape2`, can help us convert between **wide** and **tall** data frames with two functions:
	- From wide => tall: `melt`
	- From tall => wide: `dcast`

---

# Converting from wide to tall

```{r melt}
# install.packages("reshape2") # run this once, to install the package
library("reshape2")
trees_tall = melt(trees, id.vars = c("pid", "year"), 
				  variable.name = "species", 
				  value.name = "abundance")
head(trees_tall)
```

---

# Converting back to wide

```{r dcast}
# install.packages("reshape2") # run this once, to install the package
library("reshape2")
trees_wide = dcast(pid ~ year+species, data = trees_tall, value = "abundance", fill = 0)
trees_wide[1:7, 1:7]
```

# String manipulation: substr

`substr(x, i, j)`: extract a piece of a string `x`, starting in position `i` and ending in position `j`.

```{r substr}
substr("here is a string", 6, 12)
```
---

# String manipulation: substr

`substr(x, i, j)`: extract a piece of a string `x`, starting in position `i` and ending in position `j`.

```{r velo}
vel = read.csv("../data/ex4/velocity.csv")
vel[1:3, 1:7]
substr(colnames(vel)[-1], 11, 12)
```
---

# String manipulation: paste

`paste(x, y, sep = "-")`: combine x and y together into 1 string, separated by the "-" character

```{r paste}
x = "hello"
y = "world"
paste(x, y, sep = " ")
```
---

# String manipulation: pattern matching

Complex string manipulations are possible using **regular expressions**.

Useful functions: `grep`, `grepl`, `sub`, `gsub`

---

# Combining datasets: merge

Two tables can be combined based on matching **keys**

```{r width_vel_clean, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
width = read.csv("../data/ex4/width.csv")
# fix places where text was entered in numeric fields
width$width_m_1[9] = 39.4
width$width_m_1[10] = 20.8
width$width_m_2[9] = 25.4
width$width_m_2[10] = 24.6

# alternative:
# width$width_m_1 = sub("channel [12]: (\\d+)", "\\1", width$width_m_1)
# width$width_m_2 = sub("channel [12]: (\\d+)", "\\1", width$width_m_2)

# replace blanks and text with NA
width$width_m_2[width$width_m_2 == " *mean width"] = NA
width$width_m_2[width$width_m_2 == ""] = NA

# make into numbers
width$width_m_1 = as(width$width_m_1, "numeric")
width$width_m_2 = as(width$width_m_2, "numeric")


# get into tall format, remove unneeded variable column
width_clean = melt(width, id.var = "location_id", value.name = "width_m")
width_clean$variable = NULL
width_clean = width_clean[complete.cases(width_clean),]


velocity = read.csv("../data/ex4/velocity.csv")

# make it tall
velocity_clean = melt(velocity, id.vars = "location_id", value.name = "vel_m_per_s")

# extract the measurement number and drop the "variable" column
velocity_clean$measurement_number = substr(velocity_clean$variable, 11, 12)
velocity_clean$variable = NULL
velocity_clean = velocity_clean[order(velocity_clean$location_id),]
```

```{r merge_head}
head(velocity_clean)
head(width_clean)
```
---



# Combining datasets: merge

Two tables can be combined based on matching **keys**

Options to check in the help: `all.x`, `all.y`

```{r merge}
merged1 = merge(velocity_clean, width_clean, by = "location_id")
head(merged1)
```
---

# Complex aggregation: aggregate

Velocity comes with multiple measurements per location ID. `aggregate` is like a supersized `tapply` for computing statistics across different categories in a table.

```{r agg_vel_head}
head(velocity_clean)
```

---

# Complex aggregation: aggregate

Velocity comes with multiple measurements per location ID. `aggregate` is like a supersized `tapply` for computing statistics across different categories in a table.

```{r aggregate}
vel_agg = aggregate(vel_m_per_s ~ location_id, data = velocity_clean, FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
head(vel_agg)
```
